record.paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
record.original_question: How can genotype-to-phenotype predictive models, including polygenic risk scores that aggregate many weak genetic signals into an individual-level phenotype or disease-risk prediction, explain substantially more trait variance and reach clinical relevance without relying only on ever-larger cohorts?

evidence.quote: An analytical model aggregating an individual’s genotype into an overall phenotypic prediction is called a polygenic risk score (PRS) [5].

despite over a decade of refining models with exponentially increasing cohort sizes, the predictive power of most PRS is still quite poor (open problem #14: genotype-to-phenotype prediction performance).
It remains an open question whether better methodology would allow us to substantially improve PRS performance without larger cohorts.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let a quantitative or binary human phenotype Y be modeled as a function of a high-dimensional genotype vector G ∈ {0,1,2}^p (encoding allele counts at p single-nucleotide polymorphism loci, with p on the order of 10^6 to 10^7) together with unobserved environmental, demographic, and non-additive genetic factors. A polygenic risk score (PRS) is any predictor of the form Ŷ(G) = f(G; θ), where θ is learned from a training cohort of N individuals with paired (G, Y) data; the most common instance is the linear score Ŷ(G) = Σ_j β_j G_j, with weights β_j estimated from genome-wide association statistics. Predictive performance is measured by the proportion of phenotypic variance explained on held-out individuals, R²(Ŷ, Y), or by analogous metrics such as AUC for disease traits; the gap between R² and the trait's narrow-sense heritability h² quantifies the "missing prediction."

Develop methodology — for example, by exploiting non-additive interactions, rare variants, functional genomic annotations, cross-trait structure, regularization tailored to linkage disequilibrium, multi-ancestry data, or alternative model classes — such that for a fixed training cohort size N, the held-out predictive R² of the resulting PRS is substantially larger than that achievable by current linear summary-statistic-based scores, and prove quantitative guarantees on the improvement. Concretely: identify conditions on the genetic architecture of a trait (e.g., effect-size distribution, level of epistasis, sparsity, polygenicity) under which a PRS can attain R² close to h² at a sample size N strictly smaller than that required by standard additive linear models, and characterize the optimal achievable R² as a function of (N, p, h², architecture).
artifact.status_search_result: Improving polygenic risk score (PRS) accuracy without simply increasing cohort size remains an active and unsolved research problem. Recent work (2022–2025) has proposed methods incorporating functional annotations (e.g., PolyPred, LDpred-funct, PRS-CSx for cross-ancestry), but predictive R² for most complex traits remains well below heritability, and no method has been shown to close this gap at fixed N. The problem is broadly recognized as open.

status_evidence.title: Polygenic prediction via Bayesian regression and continuous shrinkage priors
status_evidence.snippet: PRS methods continue to leave a substantial gap between predicted and heritable variance for most complex traits.
status_evidence.claim: Predictive R² of PRS remains substantially below heritability across complex traits.

status_evidence.title: Genetic analyses identify widespread sex-differential participation bias and pervasive missing heritability (and related PRS reviews, 2023-2025)
status_evidence.snippet: Improving PRS accuracy without ever-larger cohorts via better statistical methodology is highlighted as an open methodological challenge.
status_evidence.claim: The methodological question of improving PRS without larger cohorts is still open.
